summary:
Tanzania criminalises same-sex sexual conduct. The Penal Code as revised by the Sexual Offences (Special Provisions) Act 1998 provides a maximum penalty of life imprisonment for same-sex acts between men; section 138A treats 'gross indecency' as an offence carrying one to five years' imprisonment or a fine of TSh 100,000 to 300,000. Heterosexual oral and anal sex are also offences under the same framework.

Zanzibar, the semi-autonomous island jurisdiction, runs a separate criminal statute. The Penal Decree Act No. 6 of 2004, enacted by Zanzibar's House of Representatives, defines 'gross indecency' broadly as any sexual act falling short of intercourse, sets sexual-offence age thresholds (absolute below 12, with under-18 and marriage distinctions) and provides penalties including three years' imprisonment. Zanzibar's Penal Code of 1934, as amended in 2004, outlaws sex between women with up to five years' imprisonment or a TSh 500,000 fine. A visitor may therefore fall under two overlapping criminal regimes depending on location.

Enforcement has been documented rather than theoretical. In 2018 the Dar es Salaam Regional Commissioner, Paul Makonda, announced a 17-member committee of police, lawyers and doctors to identify and punish homosexuals, scouring the internet for videos of people presented as LGBTQ; men detained in the resulting sweep were forced to undergo anal examinations and torture. A 2013 report by Human Rights Watch and the Wake Up and Step Forward Coalition documented torture of LGBT people in police custody, including a 19-year-old man arrested after leaving a nightclub in Mbeya who said police raped him and beat the soles of his feet with canes, electric wires and water pipes. In October 2017 the government deported staff of several HIV/AIDS organisations on the basis of 'promoting homosexuality', disrupting services.

Violence against trans people is documented. In June 2024 the UN Human Rights Office condemned as 'horrendous' the attack on Tanzanian transgender activist Mauzinde of Rahaleo, who was abducted by 12 men and found beaten in a forest with her ears cut. The office called for action against discrimination and flagged possible violations of Article 20 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and Article 13 equality guarantees in Tanzania's Constitution.

Official hostility is not confined to enforcement operations. Officials including the former president John Magufuli, Paul Makonda, Ally Hapi and Hamisi Kigwangalla have pushed persecution of LGBT people, while activists Maria Sarungi Tsehai, Fatma Karume, Mwanahamisi Singano, Carol Ndosi, Zara Kay, Khalifa Said and Goodluck Haule have publicly backed LGBT rights. Respect for freedom of speech and assembly is described as declining, and UN human rights defenders in Tanzania may not make public statements supporting tolerance for fear of reprisals. Amnesty International's January 2024 report documents escalating anti-LGBT sentiment and the weaponisation of law against LGBT people; legislation on same-sex relations was deferred after protests. The US State Department's 2013 human rights report records discrimination based on sexual orientation and describes Tanzania's human rights record as poor, with police custody abuse detailed.

State-directed online filtering constrains access to information. The Open Observatory of Network Interference documented the blocking of LGBTIQ websites, including social networks and rights sites, in Tanzania in 2024.
tangentialFactors:
The 2018 Dar es Salaam crackdown was publicly contested within the state. The Foreign Ministry said the operation lacked government support, and Denmark withheld 65 million kroner, about US$9.8 million, in aid.

Regulation of anti-LGBT hate speech has moved in both directions. The 2018 broadcast content regulations bar inciting hatred on grounds of sexual preference; the online content regulations issued the same year banned such hate speech but were completely repealed by the 2020 online content regulations. The Media Council of Tanzania's 2020 Code of Ethics for Media Professionals still bars hate speech, stereotypes and discrimination based on sexual orientation.

The US State Department's 2013 report identified the three most widespread human rights problems as excessive force by security forces, gender-based violence including female genital mutilation and cutting, and lack of access to justice, alongside societal violence against persons with albinism. These are general conditions rather than trans-specific findings.
localsOnly:
Same-sex couples have no legal recognition anywhere in Tanzania. No partner can be sponsored, inherit from, or be recognised as next of kin through relationship status. Adoption requires a married couple, so a couple whose relationship is read as same-sex under local law cannot adopt jointly.

Health policy language is non-discriminatory on paper. The 2013 National Family Planning Guidelines and Standards commit to services 'regardless of age, parity, marital status, creed, race, color, or sexual preference' and to counselling 'any woman, man, couple, or young person regardless of age'. The Nursing and Midwifery (Practice) Regulations 2010 bar withholding nursing care based on sexual orientation, and the 2017 National Guidelines for Respectful and Compassionate Nursing and Midwifery Care require non-discriminatory care. No youth-specific healthcare provision beyond the age-inclusive family planning counselling language is stated.

Tanzania has a high HIV/AIDS rate, with reportedly one million people infected.

There are no gay bars in Tanzania, although some venues exist where gay men meet. Lesbians are less visible than gay men.

Interviews with three Tanzanian LGBT activists, published in 2020, document substantial prejudice, discrimination and violence against LGBT people and denial of basic rights.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Tanzania was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); its documented finding that life imprisonment is available for same-sex activity is corroborated by other sources in this inventory.

The most recent US State Department human rights report cited here dates from 2013 and may not reflect current conditions.

Whether the 2018 Dar es Salaam crackdown carried central government backing is unresolved: the Foreign Ministry stated it did not, while the operation was announced by the regional commissioner.
